result:
Debater B's formula is correct. The maximum is max{C(n−1,2)+k, (k+1)(n−1)−1}.

**Upper bound.** By Nash-Williams–Tutte, if G has no k+1 edge-disjoint spanning trees, some partition P into p parts has at most (k+1)(p−1)−1 crossing edges. The internal edges number at most Σ C(aᵢ,2), where Σaᵢ = n and each aᵢ ≥ 1. That sum is maximized by one part of size n−p+1 and p−1 singletons. So |E(G)| ≤ f(p) = C(n−p+1,2) + (k+1)(p−1) − 1. Since f is convex in p, its maximum over 2 ≤ p ≤ n is at p=2 or p=n. These give C(n−1,2)+k and (k+1)(n−1)−1.

**Attainment.**
- For n ≥ 2k+3, take K_{n−1} plus a vertex v of degree k. The partition {v} versus the rest has only k crossing edges, so the graph fails. Adding any edge at v gives k+1 crossing edges across that cut. For every other partition, the clique K_{n−1} already satisfies the Nash-Williams condition, because n−1 ≥ 2k+2 gives at least k+1 edge-disjoint spanning trees. So the graph is τ_k-maximal with C(n−1,2)+k edges.
- For n = 2k+2, take K_n minus an edge. C(2k+2,2) = (k+1)(2k+1), so the singleton partition has (k+1)(n−1)−1 crossing edges and fails. Adding the missing edge gives K_n, which has k+1 edge-disjoint Hamiltonian paths and hence k+1 spanning trees. So this graph is τ_k-maximal with (k+1)(n−1)−1 edges.

**Consistency.** At n = 2k+3 both terms equal 2k²+4k+1. For n = 2k+2, (k+1)(n−1)−1 = 2k²+3k exceeds C(2k+1,2)+k = 2k²+2k, so the second term is the maximum there. The formula therefore gives the exact maximum for all n ≥ 2k+2.

Debater A's opening and rebuttal also defend this same formula, and A correctly rejects the undefined expression [2k+2, 4(p·t)] that was assigned to it. The only candidate with a determinate, verified value is B's formula.

DECISION: B
